questions.text: What type of images are you working with?
answers: 2D images
3D images (volumes or stacks of slices)
2D images, but I would like the results as a 3D volume
questions.help:
The purpose of this question is to determine the type of images you will use. This will help decide which deep learning model will be applied to process your images. The options are:

  • 2D images are considered those that can be represented as (x, y, channels). For example, (512, 1024, 2).

  • 3D images are those that can be represented as (x, y, z, channels). For example, (400, 400, 50, 1).

The last option, "2D images, but I would like the results as a 3D volume," refers to working with 2D images. After processing them with the deep learning model, the images will be combined in sequence to create a 3D stack. This option is useful if your 2D images together form a larger 3D volume.

questions.text: What would you like to do with your images? Choose the option that best describes what you want to achieve. See the Wizard Help for more details and examples.
answers: Identify and outline different regions or structures in the image (semantic segmentation)
Identify and outline each individual object in the image (instance segmentation)
Locate objects using points, for example, to identify the centres of nuclei (object detection)
Increase image resolution (super-resolution)
Classify images into different categories (image classification)
Remove noise from images (denoising)
Generate new images based on existing ones (image-to-image translation)
questions.help:
This question determines the type of workflow you want to run. Each option corresponds to a workflow implemented in BiaPy. The options are:

•"Identify and outline different regions or structures in the image (semantic segmentation)"  refers to the workflow called "Semantic segmentation". The goal of this workflow is to assign a class to each pixel (or voxel) of the input image, thus producing a label image with semantic masks. The simplest case would be binary classification, as in the figure depicted below. There, only two labels are present in the label image: black pixels (usually with value 0) represent the background, and white pixels represent the foreground (the wound in this case, usually labeled with 1 or 255 value).


Find more information about semantic segmentation workflow in its documentation.

•"Identify and outline each individual object in the image (instance segmentation)" refers to the workflow called "Instance segmentation". The goal of this workflow is to assign a unique ID, i.e. an integer value, to each object of the input image, thus producing a label image with instance masks. An example of this task is displayed in the figure below, with an electron microscopy image used as input (left) and its corresponding instance label image identifying each individual mitochondrion (right). Each color in the mask image corresponds to a unique object.


If your images are the frames of a time-lapse, the objects can also be tracked over time: the next question asks about it.

Find more information about instance segmentation workflow in its documentation.

•"Locate objects using points, for example, to identify the centres of nuclei (object detection)" refers to the workflow called "Detection". The goal of this workflow is to localize objects in the input image, not requiring a pixel-level class. Common strategies produce either bounding boxes containing the objects or individual points at their center of mass, which is the one adopted by BiaPy.

An example of this task is displayed in the figure below (credits to Jukkala & Jacquemet), with a fluorescence microscopy image used as input (left) and its corresponding nuclei detection results (right). Each red dot in the right image corresponds to a unique predicted object.


Find more information about detection workflow in its documentation.

•"Remove noise from images (denoising)" refers to the workflow called "Denoising". The goal of this workflow is to remove noise from the input images. BiaPy makes use of Noise2Void with any of the U-Net-like models provided. The main advantage of Noise2Void is neither relying on noise image pairs nor clean target images since frequently clean images are simply unavailable. If you do have clean versions of your noisy images, BiaPy can also use them as targets (supervised training): the Wizard will ask about it.

An example of this task is displayed in the figure below, with an noisy fluorescence image and its corresponding denoised output. This image was obtained from a Convallaria dataset used in Noise2Void project.


Find more information about denoising workflow in its documentation.

•"Increase image resolution (super-resolution)" refers to the workflow called "Super resolution". The goal of this workflow is to reconstruct high-resolution (HR) images from low-resolution (LR) ones. If there is a difference in the size of the LR and HR images, typically determined by a scale factor (x2, x4), this task is known as single-image super-resolution. If the size of the LR and HR images is the same, this task is usually referred to as image restoration.

An example of this task is displayed in the figure below, with a LR fluorescence microscopy image used as input (left) and its corresponding HR image (x2 scale factor). Credits of this image to F-actin dataset by Qiao et al.


Find more information about super-resolution workflow in its documentation.

•"Classify images into different categories (image classification)" refers to the workflow called "Classification". The goal of this workflow is to assign a label to the input image. In the figure below a few examples of this workflow's input are depicted where each image is classified as a result. Images obtained from MedMNIST v2, concretely from DermaMNIST dataset which is a large collection of multi-source dermatoscopic images of common pigmented skin lesions.


Find more information about classification workflow in its documentation.

•"Generate new images based on existing ones (image-to-image translation)" refers to the workflow called "Image to image". The goal of this workflow aims at translating/mapping input images into target images. This workflow is as the super-resolution one but with no upsampling, e.g. with the scaling factor to x1.

In the figure below an example of paired microscopy images (brightfield) is depicted. The images were obtained from Light My Cells dataset.


Find more information about image to image workflow in its documentation.

questions.text: Are your images part of a time-lapse sequence, and would you like to track objects over time?
answers: No
Yes, I want to identify objects in each frame and track them over time
questions.help:
Instance segmentation can also track the objects of a time-lapse: each frame is segmented as usual and then the objects of consecutive frames are linked, so each object keeps the same number in all the frames where it appears and cell divisions are detected. The linking is done by Trackastra {ref:trackastra}, a pretrained model that does not need to be trained on your data: in 2D its general model for live-cell images, in 3D its model trained on the Cell Tracking Challenge datasets.

If you answer Yes:

  • The training, if any, is the usual one of instance segmentation: raw images and their instance masks (e.g. some frames of your time-lapses). No tracks are needed.

  • The test folder must hold one time-lapse: one image per frame, single-channel and all of the same size, in time order when sorted by file name (e.g. t000.tif, t001.tif, ...). A time-lapse opened in Fiji can be saved like that with File > Save As > Image Sequence... Run one job per time-lapse.

  • The objects are tracked in the test phase, so the job must test the model (a training-only job just trains it).

  • The tracks are saved in the tracking folder of the results: the masks of each frame, numbered by track (mask000.tif, mask001.tif, ...), and the tracks themselves in the Cell Tracking Challenge format (res_track.txt) and as GEFF (tracks.geff).

questions.text: What would you like to do with BiaPy?
answers: Train a new AI model using my images
Use an existing AI model to analyse my images
Train a new AI model and evaluate its performance on test images
questions.help:
A deep learning model must be trained before it can be used. Training teaches it the task from images whose result you already have (the ground truth). Once trained, the model is applied to other images: BiaPy calls this phase test, and it covers two uses:

  • Prediction (also called inference): you want the results of new images, e.g. the masks of the cells in them. You only need the images.

  • Evaluation: you want to know how well the model works. You also give the ground truth of the test images, and BiaPy compares the model's results with it and reports metrics (e.g. IoU or F1). A later question asks whether you have it.

The options are:

  • Train a new AI model: only training, e.g. to apply the model later.

  • Use an existing AI model: no training. You will choose the model later: one you trained with BiaPy or a pretrained one from the BioImage Model Zoo.

  • Train a new AI model and evaluate its performance: the model is trained and then applied to test images that were not used to train it. It is evaluated if you have their ground truth; otherwise you only get its predictions.

questions.text: Do you have clean (noise-free) versions of your noisy images to use as targets?
answers: No, I only have the noisy images
Yes, I have clean target images
questions.help:
BiaPy can train a denoising model in two ways:

  • 'No, I only have the noisy images': self-supervised training with Noise2Void. Only the noisy images are needed, which is useful because clean images are frequently unavailable.

  • 'Yes, I have clean target images': supervised training. Each noisy image has a clean version of the same field of view and size, used as the target to learn from. This usually gives better results. The Wizard will ask for the folder with the clean images: they are paired with the noisy ones by file name order, so both folders must contain the same number of images.

questions.text: Could you please specify the location of the training raw image folder? Choose it (step 1) and then check its data (step 2).
questions.help:
In this step, you need to specify the folder where the images for training the network are located. All these images must have the same number of channels. It's also important that each channel contains the same type of information to avoid confusing the model.

The 'Check data' button will verify if the images within the selected folder can be read correctly by analyzing them one by one. This process may take some time, but it ensures that the images will be correctly read later in BiaPy. For this specific case, the following will be checked:

  • All images can be read properly.

  • All images have the same number of input channels.

  • All images are within the same value range. For example, if the images are in uint8 format, their values should be between 0 and 255. This must be true for all images.

questions.text: Your training images have no voxel size in their metadata. If you know it, please type it: the network is designed for it.
questions.help:
The images checked have no voxel size (the size of a voxel along Z, Y and X) in their metadata, which is common in TIFF files saved by other programs.

Microscopy stacks are often coarser along Z than in X and Y: e.g. voxels of 2 x 0.5 x 0.5 µm are 4 times taller than wide. BiaPy, like nnU-Net, designs the network for your 3D images with it: along such a Z axis the network shrinks the images less, so that it sees objects with the same proportions in all the directions. Only the proportion between Z and XY matters, so any unit works as long as the three values use the same one (BiaPy assumes µm).

You can usually find the voxel size in the microscope's acquisition settings, or in Fiji with Image > Properties... on images that still have it (e.g. the original files of the microscope). If you don't know it, leave the fields empty: the images are then taken as if their voxels were cubes or, in segmentation, the proportion is estimated from the shape of the objects in the masks.

questions.text: Could you please specify the location of the training ground truth (target) folder? Choose it (step 1) and then check its data (step 2).
questions.help:
In this step, you need to specify the directory where the training target data, also known as 'ground truth', is located. This target data will be used to train the network.

The 'Check data' button will verify that the files in the selected folder can be read properly by analyzing them one by one. This process may take some time, but it ensures that the data will be correctly read by BiaPy later.

The target and its verification vary depending on the workflow:

  • For Semantic segmentation, single-channel images are expected, specifically semantic masks. In these masks, each pixel will have a specific integer value corresponding to the class it belongs to. The checks performed include: 1) ensuring all images can be read correctly; 2) verifying that all images have the same number of input channels. Additionally, the number of classes to predict will be automatically extracted based on the different classes found in the images.
  • For Instance segmentation, one or two-channel images are expected. The first channel must always contain the instance masks, where each pixel has an integer value representing the object it belongs to. If two channels are provided, the second channel should contain the class of each instance. The checks performed include: 1) ensuring all images can be read correctly; 2) verifying that all images have the same number of input channels. If two channels are present, as in semantic segmentation, the number of classes to predict will be automatically extracted from the different classes found.
  • For Detection, files with the coordinates of object centers (centroids) are expected. The checks include: 1) ensuring the files can be read correctly; 2) verifying that the required columns for creating the coordinates are present in each file. Additionally, if the files contain a 'class' column, the number of classes will automatically be set to the highest value found in that column across all files.
  • For Super-resolution, high-resolution images are expected, meaning these images will be 2x or 4x larger than the versions in the 'Train data (raw)' folder from the previous step. The checks include: 1) ensuring all images can be read correctly; 2) verifying that all images have the same number of input channels; 3) checking that all images are within the same value range. For example, if the images are uint8, their values should be between 0 and 255 across all images.
  • For Image-to-Image, images are expected. The checks include: 1) ensuring all images can be read correctly; 2) verifying that all images have the same number of input channels; 3) checking that all images are within the same value range. For instance, if the images are uint8, the values should range between 0 and 255 across all images.

For Denoising (only when clean targets are available): the clean version of each noisy image, with the same size.

questions.text: Could you please specify the location of the test raw image folder? Choose it (step 1) and then check its data (step 2).
questions.help:
In this step, you need to specify the folder where the images for testing the network are located. All these images must have the same number of channels. It's also important that each channel contains the same type of information to avoid confusing the model.

The 'Check data' button will verify if the images within the selected folder can be read correctly by analyzing them one by one. This process may take some time, but it ensures that the images will be correctly read later in BiaPy. For this specific case, the following will be checked:

  • All images can be read properly.

  • All images have the same number of input channels.

  • All images are within the same value range. For example, if the images are in uint8 format, their values should be between 0 and 255. This must be true for all images.

questions.text: Do you have the ground truth (target) of the test images? With it, the model is also evaluated: its results are compared with the ground truth to measure how well it works.
answers: No: only predict (apply the model)
Yes: predict and evaluate the model
questions.help:
This question is meant to determine whether you have target data, or ground truth, for the test data. If you have this, BiaPy will be able to calculate various metrics, which will vary depending on the selected workflow, to measure the model's performance.

If you answer 'Yes', a follow-up question will appear, asking for the path to the target data.

questions.text: Could you please specify the location of the test ground truth (target) folder? Choose it (step 1) and then check its data (step 2).
questions.help:

  • For Instance segmentation, one or two-channel images are expected.   • For Super-resolution, high-resolution images are expected, meaning these images will be 2x or 4x larger than the versions in the 'Train data (raw)' folder from the previous step. questions.text: Your test images have no voxel size in their metadata. If you know it, please type it: it is used to compare the points detected with the ground truth ones.
questions.help:
The test images checked have no voxel size (the size of a voxel along Z, Y and X) in their metadata. When the points detected are compared with the ground truth ones, their distances along Z are scaled by it: a point one slice away is farther than one pixel away in XY when the voxels are taller than wide.

You can usually find it in the microscope's acquisition settings, or in Fiji with Image > Properties... on images that still have it. Only the proportion between Z and XY matters. If you don't know it, leave the fields empty: the voxels are then taken as cubes.

questions.text: Do you want to use a pre-trained model?
answers: No, I want to build a model from scratch
Yes, I have a model previously trained in BiaPy
Yes, I want to check if there is a pretrained model I can use
questions.help:
This question determines how the deep learning model will be built. Based on your choice, additional questions may appear to guide the model setup process.

Before using a deep learning model, it must be trained. The idea is to train the model on a specific task and then apply it to new images. For example, you could train a model to classify images based on their labels. If the training is successful, the model should be able to classify new images automatically.

Training is a crucial step to ensure good results, but it requires labeled data, also known as 'ground truth'. Using the image classification example, you would need to label the training images first, like 'image1.png' as class 1, 'image2.png' as class 2, etc. Because training can be time-consuming, using a pre-trained model can be a major advantage. A pre-trained model has already been trained on a dataset and has some level of knowledge.

If your images are similar to those used to train the pre-trained model, you might get good results without retraining it. If not, having similar images will at least make the retraining process faster and require fewer images. That's why it’s always a good idea to check for available pre-trained models that match your needs. Here are the options available:

  • 'No, I want to build a model from scratch'  This option configures BiaPy to create a model from the ground up. No additional input will be required, and BiaPy will automatically configure the model based on the selected workflow and image dimensions.

  • 'Yes, I have a model previously trained in BiaPy'  Choose this option if you already have a model trained with BiaPy. The model must be stored in the folder you’ve selected for saving results, specifically in the 'checkpoints' folder, as a file with a '.pth' extension. You’ll need to specify this file when prompted after selecting this option.

  • 'Yes, I want to check if there is a pretrained model I can use'  This option allows you to load a pre-trained model from an external source. Currently, BiaPy supports loading models from the BioImage Model Zoo. Depending on the workflow and image dimensions, you can search for compatible models to use.

questions.text: Please select the pretrained model trained with BiaPy before:
questions.help: This question is about setting the path to the pre-trained model in BiaPy. The model should be stored in the folder you previously selected for saving results. Specifically, in the 'checkpoints' folder, there will be a file with a '.pth' extension, which represents the checkpoint of the pre-trained model. You need to locate this file on your system by clicking the 'Browse' button.

questions.text: Please select a pretrained model by pressing 'Find models' below. Only the models that fit your images (dimensions and number of channels) are listed. This process requires internet connection and may take a while.
questions.help:
This question allows you to load a pre-trained model from an external source. Currently, BiaPy supports loading models from the BioImage Model Zoo.

To search for all available models, click the 'Find models' button. This will start an online search, which requires an internet connection and may take several minutes. Once the process is complete, a list will appear below the question, displaying all the pre-trained models that can be used for the selected workflow and image dimensions.

questions.text: How should the network represent the instances? The options shown suit the shape of the instances in your training masks.
answers: Foreground + contour
Foreground + central point
Foreground + distance to the border
Foreground + skeleton
Distance to the border + radial distances (StarDist)
Foreground + flows (Cellpose)
Foreground + horizontal and vertical distances (HoVer-Net)
Affinities
answer_descriptions: Binary mask of the instances plus their contours, which separate touching instances. General purpose.
Binary mask plus a point in the center of each instance, used as seed to grow it. For compact, roundish instances.
Binary mask plus, inside each instance, the distance to its border, which peaks once in the center of convex instances.
Binary mask plus the skeleton of each instance, as seed. For elongated, thin or branched instances (e.g. neurites, filaments, bacteria).
Each instance as a polygon/polyhedron from its center: distances to its border along fixed rays. Very good for crowded star-convex instances such as nuclei.
Binary mask plus a flow field that points to the center of each instance; pixels following it to the same center form an instance. Handles irregular shapes.
Binary mask plus the horizontal and vertical distances of each pixel to the center of its instance; their sharp changes separate touching instances. Designed for nuclei.

For each voxel, whether its neighbours along Z, Y and X belong to the same instance; the instances are built by merging the voxels joined by high affinities. For dense 3D instances that fill the volume, such as neurons in electron microscopy.
questions.help:
Instance segmentation networks do not predict the instances directly but an intermediate representation of them (e.g. their foreground and contours), from which the instances are built afterwards. Which one works best depends on the shape of the instances.

When the training masks were checked, the shape of their instances was measured (size, convexity, elongation, branching, how often they touch each other and whether they are star-convex, i.e. every point sees their center in a straight line). Only the representations that suit them are offered, and the recommended one is marked. The others are listed after them with the reason why they are not offered.

  • Foreground + contour: works for any shape, the contours separate touching instances.
  • Foreground + central point / distance to the border: compact, roundish instances, marked by a single point or distance peak.
  • Foreground + skeleton: elongated, thin or branched instances.
  • StarDist: star-convex instances, e.g. nuclei, even when crowded.
  • Cellpose flows: irregular, crowded cells.
  • HoVer-Net: compact instances such as nuclei in histology images.
  • Affinities: dense 3D instances that fill the volume, such as neurons in electron microscopy.

questions.text: How big should each point be when the model learns it? Every point of your annotations becomes a small disk (a ball in 3D) around it, the target the model learns to predict. Choose its radius (step 1) and, if you want, see it on your training images (step 2).
questions.help:
To learn to detect points, the model is trained to predict a small disk around each annotated point (a ball in 3D images). This question sets its radius.

  • Automatic: a quarter of the distance between the closest points of your annotations, between 1 and 5 pixels, so that the disks of neighbouring objects do not touch. That is why different datasets get different radii.

  • Manual, a radius you type in pixels: bigger disks are easier to learn and tolerate annotations that are not exactly at the center of the objects, but the disks of neighbouring objects may touch and their points merge. As a guide, use about a quarter of the size of your objects, and less than half the distance between the centers of the closest ones.

In 3D images the points become balls, whose radius along Z can differ from the one in X and Y: the voxels of microscopy stacks are often taller than wide, so an object spans fewer slices than pixels. Automatically, or if you leave it empty, the radius along Z is the one in XY scaled by the voxel size (e.g. with voxels 4 times taller than wide, 4 pixels become 1 slice). 0 marks each point only in its own slice. As a guide, type about a quarter of the number of slices your objects span.

Show the points draws the radius chosen on parts of some training images, as the model will learn it: the disks should cover the center of the objects without touching the ones of their neighbours. The summary of the configuration shows the radius used.

questions.text: How long should the training be? Only the number of training steps changes: the model and the data are the same.
answers: Quick: 2% of the training steps, for a first try
Complete: all the training steps (it can take a day)
questions.help:
How many training steps (batches of patches) the model is trained for, which decides how long it takes. Only the number of steps changes: the model, the patch size, the training images and the data augmentation are the same in both.

  • Quick: a short training, to check that the data and the configuration work, or to see how BiaPy works, e.g. in a course. In segmentation and detection it is 2% of the steps of a complete training (20 epochs instead of 1000), and it does not stop early: on a recent NVIDIA GPU about 20 minutes for 2D images and 35 minutes for 3D ones (longer on laptops, Apple Silicon or without a GPU). In the other workflows, and when a pretrained model is trained further, it is 20% of the usual number of epochs. The results are usually already reasonable, but not the best the model can give.

  • Complete: as long as nnU-Net, a reference method for biomedical segmentation, trains: 1000 epochs of 250 batches. It gives the best results but can take a day on such a GPU. It stops earlier when the model stops improving (on the validation data).

A quick training can be continued later: select the model it produced (checkpoints folder of the job) as a pretrained BiaPy model and train it again.
